slot.brief: Solve an equation reducible to a quadratic in sin x (e.g. via double-angle substitution) and express the general solution as a set.

stem: Solve $2\cos 2\theta+3\sin\theta=1$ and give the general solution, where $\alpha=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac14\right)$ and $n\in\mathbb Z$.

verdicts.working: Using \(\cos 2\theta=1-2\sin^2\theta\), the equation becomes \((4\sin\theta+1)(\sin\theta-1)=0\). Thus \(\sin\theta=1\) or \(\sin\theta=-\tfrac14\), giving the solutions in option C.

working:
Let $s=\sin\theta$. Then $2(1-2s^2)+3s=1$, so $4s^2-3s-1=0=(s-1)(4s+1)$. Thus $s=1$ or $s=-\dfrac14$. Hence $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}+2n\pi$, or $\theta=-\alpha+2n\pi$, or $\theta=\pi+\alpha+2n\pi$.

Independent check: Using \(\cos 2\theta=1-2\sin^2\theta\), the equation becomes \((4\sin\theta+1)(\sin\theta-1)=0\). Thus \(\sin\theta=1\) or \(\sin\theta=-\tfrac14\), giving the solutions in option C.
solution:
Using $\cos 2\theta=1-2\sin^2\theta$ and setting $s=\sin\theta$,
$$2(1-2s^2)+3s=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad (s-1)(4s+1)=0.$$
Thus $\sin\theta=1$ or $\sin\theta=-\frac14$. With $\alpha=\sin^{-1}(\frac14)$, the general solution is $\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}+2n\pi$, $-\alpha+2n\pi$, or $\pi+\alpha+2n\pi$, where $n\in\mathbb Z$.
